5.1.1.examLens: 5S gains fade unless something holds them in place. Know the control methods and which S has failed when the gains decay.

worked.question: After a 5S event, the area looked great. Three months later tools are back in random places, the red-tag area is overflowing, and nobody has done an audit since the event. Which S failed, and what controls would you put in place?
worked.solution: Self-Discipline (Sustain) failed. Put in place: a named area owner, a daily self-check and weekly audit with a posted scorecard, visual controls (shadow boards, floor markings) so deviations are obvious, documented standard work for the area, and regular management review of the scores.

5.1.2.examLens: Understand how a kanban works as a pull signal, and compute the number of kanbans, remembering to round up.

worked.question: Demand is 200 units per hour. Replenishment lead time is 15 minutes. The safety factor is 10%. Each container holds 25 units. How many kanbans?
worked.solution: Put lead time in hours: 15 minutes = 0.25 hour. N = 200 × 0.25 × 1.10 ÷ 25 = 55 ÷ 25 = 2.2. Round up to 3 kanbans.

5.1.3.examLens: Classify a device as a prevention (control) or warning (detection) poka-yoke, and recognize the method it uses.

worked.question: Classify each as prevention or warning, and name the method: (a) a plug that only fits one way; (b) a machine that will not start until the guard is closed; (c) an alarm that sounds if the wrong bin is picked, with no interlock; (d) a tray with 12 slots for 12 screws, where an unfilled slot is visible; (e) a sensor that blocks step 3 until step 2 is confirmed.
worked.solution: (a) Prevention, contact. (b) Prevention (interlock; a motion-step or contact-style control). (c) Warning, since it signals but does not stop the process. (d) Fixed-value (counting); it makes a missing item visible, so it is a warning type unless it also blocks the next step. (e) Prevention, motion-step (sequence).

5.1.1.a.title: Audits and checklists
5.1.1.a.html: Use a checklist scored on each S for every work area, and post the scorecard where everyone sees it. Scoring turns "it looks clean" into a number that can be tracked and compared.

5.1.1.b.title: Visual controls
5.1.1.b.html: Make the standard visible so deviations are obvious at a glance: floor markings (tape outlines for carts and bins), shadow boards (a painted outline for each tool), labels, and color coding.

5.1.1.c.title: Standard work and ownership
5.1.1.c.html: Document the standard for how each area should look and operate, and give each area a named owner who is accountable for it. Without an owner, nobody fixes drift.

5.1.1.d.title: A regular audit schedule
5.1.1.d.html: A common pattern: daily self-checks by the operators, weekly supervisor audits, and periodic management audits. Results are reviewed and acted on.

5.1.1.e.title: The gains decayed. Which S failed?
5.1.1.e.html: Self-Discipline (Sustain). The first four S's can be done in a one-time event. The fifth is the habit and the system that keeps them going.

5.1.2.a.title: A pull signal
5.1.2.a.html: A kanban is a signal (often a card or an empty container) that authorizes production or movement only when the downstream step has used material. Nothing is made or moved until the signal arrives. This is how pull systems limit inventory.

5.1.2.b.title: Card types
5.1.2.b.html:
• Production kanban: authorizes the upstream step to make more.
  • Withdrawal (move) kanban: authorizes the downstream step to take material from the upstream supply.

5.1.2.c.title: The rules
5.1.2.c.html:
• Downstream pulls from upstream, not the other way around.
  • Upstream produces only what was withdrawn.
  • No defects are passed downstream.
  • Level the load (smooth the volume and mix) so the signals stay steady.

5.1.2.d.title: The number of kanbans
5.1.2.d.html:
N = (demand × lead time × (1 + safety factor)) ÷ container size.
Demand and lead time must use the same time unit. The result must be rounded up to the next whole number, because you cannot have a fraction of a kanban.
Example: demand 120 units per day, replenishment lead time 0.5 day, safety factor 20%, container size 10. N = 120 × 0.5 × 1.2 ÷ 10 = 72 ÷ 10 = 7.2, so 8 kanbans.

5.1.2.e.title: Supermarkets and two-bin systems
5.1.2.e.html:
• A supermarket is a controlled stock location where the downstream step picks what it needs, and each pick sends a signal to replenish.
  • A two-bin system uses two containers of the same item. When one empties, it is the signal to refill while the second bin keeps work going.

5.1.2.f.title: CONWIP
5.1.2.f.html: Extension, glossary only. CONWIP (constant work in process) caps the total amount of work in a line instead of controlling each step. Low exam yield.

5.1.2.g.title: Compute N
5.1.2.g.html: Given demand, lead time, safety factor, and container size, use the formula, keep the time units the same, and round up.

5.1.3.a.title: The idea
5.1.3.a.html: Poka-yoke (mistake-proofing), from Shigeo Shingo, designs the process so an error cannot happen, or is caught immediately when it does. It does not rely on people being careful.

5.1.3.b.title: Control versus warning
5.1.3.b.html:
• Control (prevention) type: physically prevents the error or stops the process. The mistake cannot be made.
  • Warning (detection) type: signals the error (a light, buzzer, or message) but does not stop the process. A person still has to act.

Control type is stronger.

5.1.3.c.title: Methods
5.1.3.c.html:
• Contact: uses shape, size, or color to allow only the correct part or position (a part that only fits one way).
  • Fixed-value (counting): checks that the right number of items or motions occurred (a tray with a slot for each of 12 screws).
  • Motion-step (sequence): checks that steps happen in the correct order (step 3 cannot start until step 2 is confirmed).

5.1.3.d.title: Source inspection and 100% checking
5.1.3.d.html: Source inspection checks the conditions that could cause an error before the defect happens, at the source, rather than finding the defect later. Combined with 100% automatic checking at the point of the error, it prevents defects from moving forward.

5.1.3.e.title: Classify the device
5.1.3.e.html: A fixture that only accepts a part in one orientation is a prevention (control) poka-yoke using the contact method. A buzzer that sounds but does not stop the line is a warning (detection) poka-yoke.

5.1.1-1.stem: Three months after a 5S event, tools are back in random places and the red-tag area is overflowing. Nobody has audited the area since the event. Which S has failed?
5.1.1-1.explanation: The first four S's can be done in a one-time event. The fifth is the habit and system that keeps them going.

5.1.1-2.stem: Which TWO are control methods that help sustain 5S?

options.html: A scored 5S checklist audited on a regular schedule
Floor markings and shadow boards that make deviations obvious

5.1.1-2.explanation: Audits with scorecards and visual controls hold the standard in place. Larger bins and removing ownership work against it.

5.1.1-3.stem: Why is it important to assign a named owner to each 5S area?

options.html: So someone is accountable for noticing and correcting drift
So the area looks different from other areas
Because owners are required to be supervisors

5.1.2-1.stem: Demand is 90 units per hour. The replenishment lead time is 20 minutes. The safety factor is 20%, and each container holds 10 units. How many kanbans are needed?

5.1.2-2.stem: Which kanban card authorizes the upstream step to make more?
5.1.2-2.explanation: The production kanban authorizes making. The withdrawal kanban authorizes taking material from the upstream supply.

5.1.2-3.stem: In a kanban system, the upstream step produces according to a long-range forecast, regardless of what the downstream step has used.
5.1.2-3.explanation: Kanban is a pull system. The upstream step produces only what was withdrawn.

5.1.2-4.stem: A workstation has two bins of the same part. When one bin is empty, it is the signal to refill it while work continues from the second. What is this system?
5.1.2-4.explanation: An empty bin acting as the replenishment signal is a two-bin kanban system.

5.1.3-1.stem: A fixture accepts a part only when it is oriented the correct way. How is this device best classified?
5.1.3-1.explanation: The error cannot be made, so it is a control-type poka-yoke, using the contact method.

5.1.3-2.stem: A buzzer sounds when the wrong component bin is picked, but the line keeps running. How is this device best classified?
5.1.3-2.explanation: It signals the error but does not stop the process, so it is a warning-type poka-yoke.

5.1.3-3.stem: A tray has 12 slots for 12 screws, and an unfilled slot is obvious. Which poka-yoke method is this?
5.1.3-3.explanation: A check that the right number of items is present is the fixed-value method.

5.1.3-4.stem: A sensor blocks step 3 from starting until step 2 is confirmed complete. Which method and type is this?
5.1.3-4.explanation: Enforcing the correct order of steps is the motion-step method, and blocking the next step prevents the error.

5.1.3-5.stem: Which TWO statements about poka-yoke are correct?

options.html: It was developed by Shigeo Shingo
It relies on operators being careful at all times
Source inspection checks for the conditions that cause errors before the defect occurs
It applies only to final inspection

5.1.3-5.explanation: Poka-yoke is mistake-proofing that does not rely on people's care, and source inspection works at the origin of errors.

5.1.2-1.text: Demand is 90 units per hour. The replenishment lead time is 45 minutes. The safety factor is 20%, and each container holds 12 units. How many kanbans are needed?
5.1.2-1.answer: Lead time = 45 ÷ 60 = 0.750 hour. N = 90 × 0.750 × 1.20 ÷ 12 = 6.75. Round up to 7 kanbans.
